lessons.title: der Monat — "the month"
lessons.gloss: the month — and the word itself is the moon, before Rome supplied the names to put in it

segments.text: Twelve names are coming, and every one of them is Latin. The word that holds them is not.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: der Monat

segments.text: der Monat — "the month."

Say Mond and then Monat and you have heard the whole etymology. They are the same word: a month is a moon, one turn of it. English does this too — moon and month — and neither language got the idea from the other, because both inherited it.
The plural is die Monate, "the months," and it is the form the chapter title uses.
Here is the shape of the next two chapters, in one sentence.
The unit is German's own, inherited, older than any calendar: a moon. The names for the twelve are borrowed whole from Rome, along with the calendar that ordered them.
You met that division in the numbers chapter, where the counting words stayed home and the month names came in. This is where you meet the month names.

singular and plural — "der Monat, die Monate"

segments.text: "der Mond, der Monat."

Say "the month." (Der Monat.) What German word is hiding in it? (Mond, the moon.) Is Monat borrowed? (No — it is inherited.) And the twelve names about to arrive? (Latin, all of them.) Next: the first one.

lessons.title: der Januar — "January"
lessons.gloss: January — Janus, the god of doorways, which is what a first month is

segments.text: The first of the twelve borrowed names, and it is a doorway.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: der Januar

segments.text: der Januar — "January."
Latin Januarius, the month of Janus — the Roman god of doors, gateways and beginnings, shown with two faces because a doorway looks both ways at once.
A first month is exactly that: the year behind you and the year ahead, seen from the same spot.
j-as-y — German j is English y. Januar begins ya-, not ja-.
vowel-a-long — and the a that follows is long and open.
YA-nu-ar, with the weight on the first syllable.

segments.instruction: "der Januar" — YA-nu-ar
the god in it — "Janus"
what a first month is — "a door that looks both ways"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: what a first month is — "a door that looks both ways"]

segments.text: "der Januar."
Say "January." (Der Januar.) How does the j sound? (Like an English y.) Which god? (Janus, of doorways.) Why two faces? (A doorway looks both ways.) Next: a month named for a washing.

lessons.title: der Februar — "February"
lessons.gloss: February — the one month named for a ritual rather than a person or a god

segments.text: The second month, and the odd one out among the twelve.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: der Februar

segments.text: der Februar — "February."
Latin Februarius, from the Februa — a purification festival the Romans held at that point in the year, a washing-clean before the new season.
Every other month you will meet is named for a god, an emperor, or a number. This one is named for something people did.
vowel-e-german — the e of Fe- is a clear short e, not the English feb's flat vowel.
r-final — and the ending is the same soft closing r you met on Uhr.
FAY-bru-ar, four beats, weight on the first.

segments.instruction: "der Februar" — FAY-bru-ar
the first two in order — "Januar, Februar"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the first two in order — "Januar, Februar"]

segments.instruction: what it is named for — "a washing-clean"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: what it is named for — "a washing-clean"]

segments.text: "Januar, Februar."

Say "February." (Der Februar.) Is it named for a god? (No — for a festival, the Februa.) Say the first two months together. (Januar, Februar.) Next: a god you have already met, arriving a second time.

lessons.title: der März — "March"
lessons.gloss: March — Mars's month, and once the first month of the whole Roman year

segments.text: You already know something about this month from the numbers chapter, though not its name.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: der März

segments.text: der März — "March."
Latin Martius, the month of Mars, the war-god. Campaigning weather began here, and so did the Roman year.
That second fact is the one you have already been given: the Roman year opened here. Four of the twelve names still count from this month, and you will meet them in the next chapter.
vowel-ae — ä is a bright open e, close to English bed. Not the ar of English March.
tz-affricate — and -rz ends on a ts, so the word closes merts.

segments.instruction: "der März" — merts
the god — "Mars"
three in order — "Januar, Februar, März"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: three in order — "Januar, Februar, März"]

segments.text: "der März."
Say "March." (Der März.) How does -rz end? (On a ts.) Which god? (Mars.) Where did the Roman year begin? (Here, in March.) Next: the same god, under a name you already own.

lessons.title: März and Dienstag
lessons.gloss: one god, two doors into German — borrowed by name in März, translated by name in Dienstag

segments.text: Two German words you now own. They come from the same god, and neither of them looks like the other.
Mars entered German twice, and by two different routes.

utterances: the route: his name, borrowed whole. what German got: Latin Martius. result: März.
the route: his job, given to Tiw. what German got: Germanic Tiwaz. result: Dienstag.

segments.text: When the Romans met the Germanic gods, they matched them up by what they did: the war-god here answers the war-god there. Tuesday was Mars's day, so it became Tiw's day, and it still is — in German Dienstag, in English Tuesday.
The month got no such treatment. Nobody translated Martius; German took it as it stood.
The difference is worth holding onto, because it is the whole chapter in one example.

The week was a thing Germanic speakers already had, so when the Roman scheme arrived they mapped it onto their own gods and kept their own words. The calendar of twelve months was not; it came in as an administrative object, name-plates and all, and German took the name-plates.
Same god, same century, two outcomes — decided by whether German already had something to put in the slot.

segments.instruction: the pair — "März, Dienstag"
what each did with the god — "took his name; took his job"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: what each did with the god — "took his name; took his job"]

segments.instruction: the reason — "German had a week already; it had no twelve months"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the reason — "German had a week already; it had no twelve months"]

segments.text: "März and Dienstag — one god, two doors."

Which two German words carry Mars? (März and Dienstag.) Which took his name? (März.) Which took his job? (Dienstag, through Tiw.) Why did the week get translated and the calendar not? (German already had a week.) Next: a month that may be named for an opening.

lessons.title: der April — "April"
lessons.gloss: April — the one month whose Roman name nobody can be sure about

segments.text: Three months in and every name has had an owner. This one does not.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: der April

segments.text: der April — "April."
Latin Aprilis. Where that came from is genuinely unsettled — the Romans of the classical period were already guessing. The oldest and best guess is aperire, "to open," for the month when things do.
Say it aloud and notice where the weight sits: German puts it on the second syllable, a-PRIL, where English puts it on the first.
r-uvular — the r in -pril is made at the back of the throat, closer to a soft scrape than an English roll.
i-short — and the i is short and bright: pril, not preel.

segments.instruction: "der April" — a-PRIL, weight at the back
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "der April" — a-PRIL, weight at the back]

segments.instruction: the guess — "aperire, to open"
four in order — "Januar, Februar, März, April"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: four in order — "Januar, Februar, März, April"]

segments.text: "der April."
Say "April." (Der April.) Which syllable carries the weight? (The second — a-PRIL.) Who is it named for? (Nobody knows — perhaps aperire, "to open".) Next: a goddess of growing things.

lessons.title: der Mai — "May"
lessons.gloss: May — Maia, a goddess of growth, and the shortest month name German has

segments.text: One syllable, and its vowel is one you were given for a number.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: der Mai

segments.text: der Mai — "May."
Latin Maius, the month of Maia — a goddess of growth and increase, which is a reasonable thing to call the month when everything is putting on size.
ai-as-eye — ai is the vowel of English eye.
You already have that vowel under its commoner German spelling, ei, from the numbers. German writes the same sound two ways, and Mai is the rarer one: ei and ai both say eye.
So Mai rhymes with English my.

segments.instruction: "der Mai" — rhymes with "my"
the goddess — "Maia, of growing things"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the goddess — "Maia, of growing things"]

segments.instruction: five in order — "Januar, Februar, März, April, Mai"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: five in order — "Januar, Februar, März, April, Mai"]

segments.text: "der Mai."
Say "May." (Der Mai.) What does ai sound like? (English eye.) Which other spelling gives that sound? (Ei.) Which goddess? (Maia.) Next: the queen of the gods.

lessons.title: der Juni — "June"
lessons.gloss: June — Juno, queen of the gods, and a j that sounds like Januar's

segments.text: Its first letter behaves exactly as the first month's did.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: der Juni

segments.text: der Juni — "June."
Latin Junius, the month of Juno — Jupiter's queen, and the goddess Romans married under, which is why June weddings are a Roman habit that never stopped.
j-as-y — the same j as Januar: English y. YOO-ni, never joon.
ie-long-ee — and the final i is a long ee.
Spoken German often lengthens this one to Juno when a date has to be clear over the phone, because the month after it sounds far too close. That is a real habit, not something you have to learn now.

segments.instruction: "der Juni" — YOO-nee
the goddess — "Juno"

segments.source: [YOU SAY: six in order — "Januar, Februar, März, April, Mai, Juni"]

segments.text: "der Juni."
Say "June." (Der Juni.) How does the j sound? (Like English y.) Which other month opens the same way? (Januar.) Which goddess? (Juno.) Next: all six, said through.

lessons.title: Practice — half a Roman year
lessons.gloss: chapter payoff — the inherited unit, the borrowed names, and the god who came in twice

segments.text: No new words. Six names and the container they sit in.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: what German owns and what it bought

utterances: what: the unit. German: der Monat. where from: inherited — it is der Mond.
what: the names. German: Januar … Juni. where from: Latin, taken whole.

segments.text: One line, and it is the chapter. German had a moon and needed no help naming the span. It had no twelve-month calendar, so when one arrived it took the labels that came with it.
Notice what the six names are for, because they are not one kind of thing:
Januar — a god, Janus of doorways.
Februar — not a god at all, but a festival, the Februa.
März — a god, Mars, who is also in Dienstag under another name.
April — unknown, and unknown already in Rome.
Mai — a goddess, Maia of growth.
Juni — a goddess, Juno, queen of the gods.
Four deities, one ritual, one shrug. A calendar is not a designed object; it is a pile of things people happened to call months, kept because nobody stopped.

segments.text: "Januar, Februar, März, April, Mai, Juni."

Say the first six months. (Januar, Februar, März, April, Mai, Juni.) Which word for the span is German's own? (Der Monat, from Mond.) Which month shares a god with Dienstag? (März.) Which one is named for a festival? (Februar.) Which one nobody can explain? (April.)
